opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the underrated dynamics in thinking about AI control and insider risk at AI companies.

Right now, a big constraint on AI research is human labour. You've got some number of researchers, and each of them can only run so many experiments, read so many results, write so much code. Compute matters a lot, but the binding constraint for a lot of research is researcher time and attention. So the access patterns we have today reflect that. Researchers get fairly broad permissions, because the main cost of restricting them is that you slow down a scarce, expensive human.

Once you have AI systems that can do a lot of the research labour, that ratio flips. Suddenly labour is cheap and abundant: you can spin up thousands of instances of an AI agent. Compute becomes the much more binding constraint. I think that changes the access question in a few ways.

First, the amount of access in aggregate goes way up. If you have huge numbers of AI researchers each running experiments, they collectively touch a lot more of your infrastructure, code, and potentially model weights than your human staff ever did. So whatever risk you think comes from giving one agent a given level of access, you have to multiply it.

Second, and more hopefully, I think it actually makes fine-grained access control more affordable. When labour was scarce, it was really costly to make a researcher jump through hoops: request permissions, wait for review, work in a sandbox. When labour is cheap, the cost of an agent waiting, or doing things a slightly less convenient way, is much lower. Compute is what you're trying not to waste. So you can afford to design workflows where AIs operate with much more restricted, task-specific permissions, where actions get monitored or reviewed, where you route the risky stuff through more trusted pathways. That's much more viable when you're not burning expensive human hours.

Third, a lot of what AI researchers need access to is fundamentally about using compute: launching jobs, running training runs, accessing data and checkpoints. So the security-relevant question shifts toward: how do you let AIs efficiently use lots of compute for legitimate experiments, without giving them the ability to, say, exfiltrate weights, tamper with training of their successors, or launch unmonitored jobs? I think that's tractable in a lot of cases, because most experiments don't actually need the dangerous permissions. You can often give access to a narrow API for submitting jobs rather than raw access to the cluster.

So my overall take is that the changing ratio is a mixed bag. It massively increases the attack surface and the stakes, but it also changes the economics in a way that makes the kinds of control measures I'm excited about less costly than people might naively expect. A lot of the work is figuring out, ahead of time, which permissions are actually needed for productive research and which can be locked down, so that when AI labour gets cheap, labs don't just default to handing out the same broad access they give human researchers today.

r001.rationale: The response says labour will become abundant and compute more constrained, but does not predict that AI researchers will spend labour to improve compute efficiency.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss recovering useful results from flawed experiments as an alternative to rerunning them.

r003.rationale: It mentions narrow APIs for submitting jobs, but not GPU sharing or substantial software for coordinating experiments.

r004.rationale: The response raises model weights as something agents might access or exfiltrate, but does not state that AI researchers will necessarily have access to dangerously capable AIs' weights.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more underappreciated dynamics here. Right now, if you look at how AI research happens at a frontier lab, you've got a bunch of humans who have a lot of latitude. They can run experiments, they can poke at the model weights, they can look at training data, they can SSH into boxes and do pretty arbitrary things. And the reason they have that access is basically that they need it to do their jobs, and there aren't that many of them, so it's manageable from a security perspective.

But I think the picture changes a lot once AIs are doing a large fraction of the research. The ratio of labour to compute shifts — you have way more "researcher-hours" relative to the amount of compute, because AI labour is cheap. And that has a couple of implications.

One is that each individual unit of research labour is less valuable, so you can afford to constrain it more. If a human researcher has to wait two hours for a security review before running an experiment, that's a huge productivity hit. If an AI agent has to go through some automated check, or has to run inside a sandbox where it can't touch the weights directly, that's a much smaller cost relative to the total throughput you're getting. So I think you can — and should — be a lot stingier with what you give the AIs access to.

The other implication is that the threat model changes. With human researchers, you're mostly worried about a small number of insiders or an external attacker compromising someone's credentials. With AI researchers, you have to worry about the possibility that the models themselves are misaligned and are going to try to use their access to do something you don't want — exfiltrate weights, sabotage safety research, insert backdoors into the next generation of models, whatever. And because there are so many instances doing so many things, you can't really have a human look at each action.

So my view is that the access AI researchers need is actually much narrower than what human researchers currently have, and labs should be designing their infrastructure around that. You want the AIs to be able to propose experiments, run code on isolated compute, read results, and so on — but you probably don't want them to have direct access to production weights, or the ability to modify training pipelines without some kind of oversight, or unrestricted network access. A lot of what we think about in AI control is basically: how do you set up the permissions and monitoring so that even if the model is trying to screw you over, it can't do much damage, while still letting it do useful research?

And I think the nice thing is that this gets easier, not harder, as compute becomes the bottleneck. When you have more labour than you know what to do with, you can afford to burn some of it on redundancy — having multiple models check each other's work, having a trusted weaker model review the actions of a more capable untrusted one, that kind of thing. The constraint is compute, not clever ideas, so you can spend a lot of cheap AI effort on oversight.

r001.rationale: The response says AI labour will be abundant relative to compute and may be spent on oversight, but does not predict spending labour to improve compute efficiency.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss recovering useful results from flawed experiments as an alternative to rerunning them.

r003.rationale: It does not mention sharing GPUs or having AI researchers write software to coordinate experiments.

r004.rationale: The response says AI researchers probably should not have direct access to production weights, rather than claiming they necessarily will.

astra-6.text:
I think as the labour gets cheaper relative to the compute, researchers will increasingly need access to large amounts of compute to do useful experiments. If you can get an AI to do a lot of the implementation and analysis, then having a clever idea and the ability to write the code stops being as much of an advantage. The scarce resource becomes being able to run the experiment.

That could make it harder to do relevant research outside the big AI companies. You might have access to a very capable AI research assistant, but that doesn’t mean you have the budget to run the experiments it proposes. And access to a model through an API isn’t necessarily enough—you might need to modify its training or inspect what’s happening inside it.

So I’d expect access to compute, and access to models in a form that lets you experiment with them, to become more important relative to access to human research labour. There’ll still be useful cheap experiments, but I wouldn’t assume that making the intellectual work cheaper automatically makes the whole research process more accessible.

r001.rationale: The response says compute will become more important as labour gets cheaper, but does not predict researchers will spend more labour to improve compute efficiency.

r002.rationale: It does not mention recovering useful results from flawed experiments as an alternative to rerunning them.

r003.rationale: It discusses access to compute and models, but not GPU sharing or AI-written coordination software.

r004.rationale: The response says researchers may need models they can modify or inspect; it does not state they will necessarily have access to dangerous AIs’ weights.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how much human labour you need to turn a given amount of compute into useful research. At the moment, doing an AI experiment involves a bunch of researcher time: deciding what to try, writing the code, looking at the results, figuring out what went wrong. If AI systems can do more of that work, you can run many more experiments with the same number of human researchers, and compute becomes a larger fraction of the cost.

That could make access to compute much more important for being at the research frontier. You might have a really good idea, but the thing you’re competing against is a lab that can have AI researchers explore thousands of variations on its ideas.

But I’d distinguish access to a powerful model from access to everything involved in developing it. For some research, being able to query the model might be enough. For other research, you need to inspect its internals or modify its weights or run training experiments. So I don’t think there’s one answer to how much access researchers need. It depends on which parts of the research process get automated and what kinds of experiments you’re trying to do.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could let researchers run more experiments with the same number of people, but does not predict they will spend more labour to improve compute efficiency.

r002.rationale: It mentions figuring out what went wrong in experiments, but does not identify recovering useful results as an alternative to rerunning them.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss AI researchers sharing GPUs or writing software to coordinate experiments.

r004.rationale: It says some research may require access to weights, but does not state that researchers will necessarily have access to weights of dangerously capable AIs.
